title: Greedflation Is Real
summary: Josh and Chuck examine "greedflation," the idea that companies used the COVID-19 pandemic and related supply shocks to raise prices and profit margins beyond what costs justified. They cover the standard explanations (pandemic supply chain disruptions, stimulus checks, avian flu egg shortages, the war in Ukraine), grocery price increases, food company and grocery store profits, the Economic Policy Institute cost breakdown, shrinkflation and skimpflation, the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City's "early price hikes" paper, counterarguments such as Eric Levitz's critique, and policy options like price controls and windfall profit taxes. The episode closes with a listener mail segment and sign-off.

segments.title: Live tour dates and opening
segments.summary: Hosts announce 2024 live tour dates and tickets information, then the show's opening credits.

segments.title: Framing the greedflation debate
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce greedflation as a new term and frame the debate over whether record food company profits go beyond normal capitalism or raise a moral question.

segments.title: Scale of grocery price increases
segments.summary: Food inflation at US grocery stores rose 11.4 percent in 2022 and about 5 percent in 2023, against a normal annual rate of about 2.5 percent, for nearly 17 percent over two years.

segments.title: Standard explanations: pandemic, supply chains, stimulus
segments.summary: The hosts review commonly cited causes: pandemic supply chain disruptions and ingredient and packaging shortages (including a caffeine free Coke shortage tied to aluminum), higher demand from people eating at home, and stimulus checks, noting Europe had similar inflation without stimulus checks.

segments.title: Avian flu, Ukraine war and global interconnection
segments.summary: Avian flu killed hens and reduced egg and poultry supply, and egg prices later fell as flocks recovered. The war in Ukraine disrupted wheat exports and energy prices, raising costs for imported goods.

segments.title: Walking through a grocery store
segments.summary: Using a comedic grocery store walk-through, the hosts cite USDA figures: food up 25 percent from 2019 to 2023, with bread, flour, butter, nuts and snack foods rising sharply, and Halloween candy prices up sharply.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Regressive impact on low-income families
segments.summary: Food price increases hit low-income households and poor countries hardest because they spend a larger share of their budgets on food, pushing some people into poverty.

segments.title: Global Food Price Index and concentrated food corporations
segments.summary: The Food Price Index's five categories rose 57 percent from 2020 to 2022 worldwide, with some prices like eggs later falling. The hosts note a handful of large corporations own most food brands.

segments.title: Corporate profits rising faster than costs
segments.summary: Tyson Foods reportedly doubled its profits year over year in early 2022, and Gill (Conagra-era reference unclear in transcript) reported record profits. Food corporations recorded their largest profits in about seventy years during peak inflation.

segments.title: General Mills profits despite falling sales
segments.summary: General Mills sales declined in 2021 and 2022 yet its profits rose sharply, which the hosts cite as documented evidence of profiteering.

segments.title: Food billionaires
segments.summary: Oxfam counted 62 new food billionaires from 2020 to 2022, who made more money during the two pandemic years than in the previous 23 years combined.

segments.title: Economic Policy Institute cost breakdown
segments.summary: The Economic Policy Institute splits price increases into unit labor costs, non-labor costs, and profit margins. Over forty years labor accounted for about 62 percent of inflation, non-labor 27 percent and profit about 11.4 percent. Since 2020, labor fell below 8 percent, non-labor rose to 38 percent, and profit rose to nearly 54 percent.

segments.title: Seller's inflation and monetary policy
segments.summary: Chuck and Josh discuss the earlier term seller's inflation, coined by economist Abraham Lerner in 1958, and contrast Keynesian and classical views, noting Federal Reserve interest rate hikes do not control corporate pricing decisions.

segments.title: Why competition broke down during the pandemic
segments.summary: Normally competitors restrain price increases because shoppers switch brands. During the pandemic, shared supply shocks gave companies cover to raise prices together without explicit collusion, and consolidation reduced competition; three companies reportedly make 70 to 80 percent of cereal in US stores.

segments.title: Earnings calls and CEO admissions
segments.summary: The Groundwork Collaborative reviewed corporate earnings calls where executives described the pandemic as a chance to reset prices. A ConAgra executive reportedly said consumers would welcome the price increase.

segments.title: Consumers accepting higher prices
segments.summary: Hosts argue that consumers continuing to buy at higher prices signals companies that the new price is acceptable, prompting further increases, until demand falls. Lower-income people feel the most pressure.

segments.title: Gas prices and new normal baselines
segments.summary: Chuck recalls gas prices jumping around 2000 and remaining high. Josh explains that prices rise and rarely fall back, so pandemic-era increases may have reset the baseline, and suggests higher prices may now be driving inflation.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Mid-episode ad break.

segments.title: Grocery store profits
segments.summary: Grocery stores have departments that estimate food producers' costs to check markups, but the FTC studied nine grocery stores and wholesalers, including Kroger, Amazon and Walmart, and found industry profits rising out of step with costs, from a peak markup of 5.6 percent in 2015 to over 7 percent two years later.

segments.title: Shrinkflation and skimpflation
segments.summary: Shrinkflation means paying the same price for less product, while skimpflation means ingredients or packaging are downgraded to save money, which is not tracked in official inflation measures.

segments.title: Kansas City Fed on early price hikes
segments.summary: Economists at the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City found large price hikes began in 2020 and early 2021, before inflation peaked in late 2021 and 2022, suggesting firms anticipated higher costs. Sticky prices and downward rigidity mean prices rarely fall as costs drop.

segments.title: Counterarguments: Eric Levitz and the 'backwards' view
segments.summary: Eric Levitz of New York Magazine argued consolidation predated the pandemic and that inflation caused higher profits, not the reverse. Robert Reich responded that the pandemic gave cover for price increases. Levitz concluded that pandemic conditions and checks caused the problem.

segments.title: Price controls and windfall profit taxes
segments.summary: An economist at Societe Generale (name uncertain in transcript) called the corporate greed unprecedented and suggested price controls. Josh says price controls can cause shortages and proposes a higher tax on windfall profits, with Chuck asking about triggers.

segments.title: Corporate purpose and whether profits should be shared
segments.summary: Chuck argues that windfall profits get passed to workers and consumers; Josh disagrees and says corporations focused only on shareholder profit are a problem. Both agree food is an essential good, unlike luxury items.

segments.title: Hosts' view and audience reaction
segments.summary: The hosts acknowledge listeners may disagree and invite opinions and other solutions.

segments.title: Listener mail from Daniel
segments.summary: Listener Daniel Klein writes about listening during long drives, asks for a shout-out to his wife Lynn, and mentions his kids enjoy the show and that he is working through episodes from newest to oldest; he also recommends the Dave Ruse podcast Biblical Time Machine. Josh gives a contact email.
